meta.notes: Both Dark Side of the Boom posts are paywalled previews; items are based on the bulleted takeaways plus the intro text. The Unchained episode is a paywalled video; items are based on the show notes.

items.source: Unchained / Laura Shin (guest: Jonah Erlich, Den)
items.title: Hacks moved from smart-contract bugs to opsec and cloud infra: wallet security is now a key-architecture problem
items.idea: Erlich argues most crypto hacks have shifted from smart-contract bugs to operational-security and cloud-infrastructure compromises (Drift malware as the case study). Den's MLS Wallet, publicly launched Nov 11 after going live with design partners in June, checks transaction policies three separate times: on the signer's device, at an isolated guardian co-signer, and in onchain contracts monitored in real time. It uses separate keys with separate jobs rather than shards of one MPC key, recovery runs on an encrypted seed backup that Den can't decrypt, and pricing is annual contracts, not volume-based.
items.angle: The attack surface has moved from code to people and cloud. That favors custody/infra vendors priced like SaaS, and it means audit-firm-style 'contract verified' badges are losing their value as a safety signal for DeFi exposure.
items.tweetA: The smart contract was never the weak link. The laptop and the AWS account were. If most hacks are now opsec and cloud compromises, a 'fully audited' badge tells you almost nothing about whether your treasury survives a phished signer.
items.tweetB: Interesting pricing detail: annual contracts, no per-volume fees. Custody is turning into enterprise SaaS. Whoever wins institutional wallet infra gets paid like Okta, not like an exchange, and that's a much steadier business than the trading cycle.

charts.desc: Episode header image only, no data charts.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / UBS Keith Parker
items.title: UBS leans 'buy the dip' after an 11%+ S&P correction, with AI prices and AI fundamentals pulling apart
items.idea: After an S&P 500 correction of more than 11%, a sharp cut in speculative exposure and some of the year's most extreme volatility readings, UBS's US equity strategy team (Buy or Fade? Assessing the Setup Amid the Volatility) leans toward buying weakness rather than fading rallies. Their key point is that AI equities have been punished while capex and earnings expectations stay 'remarkably resilient', so share prices and fundamentals are diverging. Volatility, valuations and positioning now support a recovery. The bond market does not agree.
items.angle: When prices fall but EPS and capex revisions don't, the selloff is about the multiple, not the business. The thing to watch is whether credit validates the equity bottom; equity strategists alone won't.
items.tweetA: Price down 11%+, capex expectations unchanged, earnings expectations unchanged. Either the sell side's numbers are about to get cut hard, or this is a multiple reset that buyers will look back on fondly. I'd watch revisions breadth over the next 3 weeks, not the strategists.
items.tweetB: Equity strategists say buy. The bond market says not yet. In 2018 the credit market was right and the equity bulls were early by about a month. The December FOMC is where that disagreement gets settled.

charts.desc: Header image in the email. The full post probably has UBS positioning/vol charts. Charts inside, worth opening.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / UBS Keith Parker
items.title: 'Credit holds the key to another 2018': can the AI infra boom keep financing itself on shareholder-friendly terms?
items.idea: The UBS note frames the setup against 2018 and says credit, not equity positioning, is the swing factor. Credit investors are starting to ask whether the AI infrastructure boom can keep financing itself 'on the terms shareholders have come to expect', which means cheap debt alongside buybacks. The December Fed meeting is flagged as the key test.
items.angle: If spreads on AI-capex issuers widen while equities bounce, the bounce is a bear-market rally. The real 2018 analogue is the Q4 credit-led drawdown, not the February vol event.
items.tweetA: The 2018 analogue people keep missing: equities bottomed in Feb, then credit cracked in Q4 and took everything down 20%. If AI capex funding costs reprice now, the dip buyers are buying the February low of a December problem.
items.tweetB: The question isn't whether hyperscalers can afford the capex. It's whether they can afford capex AND buybacks AND IG-tight spreads at the same time. Something in that trio gives in 2027, and equity holders assume it won't be them.

items.title: Jensen reinstated 11 days after resigning, after the President dialed in. NVDA +31%, ~$1T, the largest one-day value gain on record
items.idea: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned, following a board meeting the President dialed into (per The Information). The AG had told the President there was no evidence of wrongdoing, the VP relayed this to the board, and the vote was unanimous (Semafor). NVDA jumped 31%, regaining nearly $1T, the largest one-day market-value gain on record for a US company (WSJ). Huang then told staff Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan (CNBC) while running about 60 direct reports, and the President said a pardon is 'always an option'.
items.angle: Key-person risk at the world's most important AI supplier is now also political-patronage risk. That should carry a governance discount, and Parekh says credit is pricing one before equity does.
items.tweetA: $1T of market cap came back in one session because of one phone call from the White House. That's not a governance story anymore. It's a sovereign-backstop story, and NVDA now trades partly as a political asset.
items.tweetB: Do the math: +31% for ~$1T means the market priced Jensen alone at roughly a quarter of Nvidia's value. And he just said there's no need for a succession plan, with 60 direct reports. The key-person discount is real and almost nobody is hedging it.

charts.desc: About 6 embedded images (post art, episode graphics). No standalone data chart identified in the email body.

items.title: S&P puts Nvidia's AA on watch for a downgrade over governance. Moody's cuts its outlook. NVDA CDS at a record
items.idea: After the reinstatement, S&P placed Nvidia's AA rating on watch for a possible one-notch downgrade, citing governance. Moody's cut its outlook to stable, and the cost of insuring Nvidia's debt hit a record (ZeroHedge). Parekh's read: the raters are the first to price the 'one-man show', and others will follow across the ecosystem Nvidia finances.
items.angle: Nvidia's balance sheet indirectly backstops neoclouds and vendor-financing deals. A wider NVDA credit spread passes through to CoreWeave-style borrowers and AI infra ABS.
items.tweetA: Equity forgave Jensen in a day. Credit didn't: S&P watch-negative, Moody's outlook cut, CDS at a record. When the bond market and the stock disagree on the same headline, I trust the side that has to get paid back.
items.tweetB: The second-order effect nobody's pricing: Nvidia is the implicit guarantor behind a lot of neocloud and GPU-backed financing. If NVDA's own credit gets repriced on governance, the whole vendor-financing stack gets more expensive. $NVDA $CRWV

items.title: Many Anthropic and OpenAI staff no longer think their best internal models can be safely released
items.idea: Per Axios (more than two dozen sources), many employees at Anthropic and OpenAI no longer believe their most capable internal models can be safely released. Internal debate ranges from keeping frontier models for internal use only to whether to train new ones at all. Parekh's datapoint: one Anthropic research run used 31 million tokens in about 36 hours, roughly 10x what a maxed-out $200/month plan gets, on models the public can't buy. With governments not forcing a slowdown, self-imposed restraint may be the main brake (Dario Amodei, 'We Must Pace the Frontier').
items.angle: If frontier capability stays internal, the lab's moat becomes 'what we use ourselves' rather than 'what we sell', and the gap between public benchmarks and true capability widens. That's bearish for anyone underwriting AI on public-model performance alone.
items.tweetA: 31M tokens in 36 hours is about 240 tokens a second, nonstop, for a day and a half, from a single research run. The people inside the labs aren't using the same AI you are. That gap is the real information asymmetry in this market.
items.tweetB: New supply-side risk for the AI trade: what if the best models simply don't ship? A lab that keeps its frontier model internal still needs the compute but monetizes it less directly. Capex keeps going and public product revenue lags. That's the worst mix for the multiple.

items.title: Anthropic $81B run rate vs OpenAI ~$70B. Compute commitments $895B vs $750B. Both ~$1.2T. Tied on Epoch's index
items.idea: Four years after ChatGPT, the two labs' best public models are tied at about 174 on Epoch AI's capability index. Anthropic's annualized run rate ($81B) is ahead of OpenAI's (heading to about $70B), and its compute commitments are bigger (about $895B vs $750B). Valuations are roughly even: OpenAI's last private round was $1.25T, and Anthropic is about $1.2T in the public market after its November IPO. OpenAI's IPO countdown is aimed at 2027 (WSJ). Parekh calls it 'Coke and Pepsi, flipped.'
items.angle: The multiples tell you who has more to prove: Anthropic at about 14.8x run rate, OpenAI at about 17.9x. Compute commitments of about 11x revenue at both labs make them the two largest single sources of demand for the GPU/HBM/power stack.
items.tweetA: Anthropic: $1.2T on $81B run rate = ~14.8x. OpenAI: $1.25T on ~$70B = ~17.9x. The company that's ahead on revenue is the cheaper one, and it's the one you can actually buy. The 2027 OpenAI IPO has to explain that gap.
items.tweetB: The number that matters for semis: $895B + $750B = ~$1.65T in compute commitments from two companies with ~$150B of combined revenue. That's 11x revenue owed to the GPU/HBM/power stack. Supplier backlogs are underwritten by two balance sheets.

items.title: SpaceX + Tesla: a potential $3.5T merger by year-end. Musk could control about 74% of the votes
items.idea: Five directors (two from SpaceX, three from Tesla) on two special committees are negotiating what could be the biggest merger ever, a potential $3.5T combination racing toward a deal by year-end (FT). Elon is CEO of both and officially not in the room. Three issues decide it: the exchange ratio, Elon's opinions, and governance. His supervoting shares give him about 84% of the votes at SpaceX vs about 20% at Tesla, and Parekh's rough math puts him at about 74% of the combined company's votes if SpaceX's structure carries over. It would complete the year's 'mega-AI IPO troika': SpaceX/xAI public in June, Anthropic in November, OpenAI in 2027.
items.angle: Tesla public shareholders would swap a 20%-controlled company for a 74%-controlled one. The exchange ratio is effectively the price of giving up governance, and index providers' rules on dual-class shares become a live flow question.
items.tweetA: Tesla holders go from a CEO with ~20% of the votes to one with ~74%. Whatever exchange ratio the committee lands on, part of it is the price of a governance downgrade. I'd want a big premium for that, and I doubt Tesla holders get one. $TSLA
items.tweetB: A $3.5T merged entity with ~74% voting control in one person tests every index provider's dual-class rules at once. The passive-flow math on this deal may matter more than the synergy math.

items.title: 'RAMageddon' hits holiday shopping: gadget prices are rising and sticking
items.idea: AI-driven memory demand ('RAMageddon') is pushing up consumer gadget prices into the holiday season, and Parekh argues the higher prices will stick. An ARD episode adds that Black Friday shoppers are settling for 'good-enough gadgets'.
items.angle: Higher memory pricing is reaching the consumer price level. That supports DRAM/HBM pricing power ($MU, SK Hynix, Samsung), but it hurts unit volumes for PC/phone OEMs, and it's a small but real goods-inflation input.
items.tweetA: AI capex just showed up at the Best Buy checkout. When HBM eats the wafer supply, the DRAM in your laptop gets pricier. Memory makers win either way, and OEM margins absorb what consumers won't. $MU
items.tweetB: 'Good-enough gadgets' on Black Friday is the consumer-side tell. People are trading down on specs because memory got expensive. If that holds into Q1, PC/phone unit guidance is too high, even as memory revenue beats.

items.title: New tariff wave on China, and 'China's growing US Tech Eclipse' as chip, remote-access and distillation doors shut at once
items.idea: ARD #213 covers a new tariff wave on China. Sunday's 'Bigger Picture' preview frames a growing Chinese tech eclipse of the US, led by Huawei, as three doors close at once: chip exports, remote (cloud) compute access, and model distillation. Congress is also said to be eyeing AI rules (ARD #216).
items.angle: Closing all three channels at once forces China to build a fully domestic stack. That accelerates Huawei Ascend and SMIC, and it shrinks the long-run China TAM for US AI vendors faster than the tariff headlines suggest.
items.tweetA: Chips, remote compute and distillation shut at the same time. That's not export control anymore, it's full decoupling of the AI stack. Every door you close is a subsidy to Huawei's roadmap.
items.tweetB: The underrated part is distillation. Blocking chips slows training. Blocking distillation stops China from copying the output of US frontier models. If that actually holds, the capability gap could widen, or it pushes China's labs to innovate on efficiency, which is how DeepSeek happened.

items.title: 'Handoverism': who owns the agents, and who decides, when billions of AIs do the work
items.idea: A three-part series on 'Handoverism', the debate over ownership and decision rights once billions of AI agents do economic work. It was sparked by essays like 'Against Against Handover'. The core question is whether humans hand over decision authority, not just tasks.
items.angle: Ownership of agents is the next property-rights fight: who captures the surplus, whether that's the model owner, the deployer or the user. That's the political-economy layer under every 'AI replaces labor' thesis.
items.tweetA: The labor debate asks 'will AI take jobs?' The better question is who owns the agent that took the job. Whoever holds the rights to the agent captures the wage, and that's a capital-vs-labor shift dressed up as a tech story.
items.tweetB: 'Handover' is a governance problem before it's a technical one. Companies already struggle to audit human decisions. Auditing a billion agent decisions per day is a whole new compliance industry. Somebody is going to build the Big Four of agent audit.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Sachs Tony Pasquariello
items.title: After 'one of the biggest liquidations of his career', GS's Pasquariello says the uptrend holds, but the AI trade has changed
items.idea: Pasquariello sees a market in better technical shape after November's liquidation: machines sold, hedge funds cut exposure, and downside hedges were unwound into the Thanksgiving rally. The primary equity uptrend remains intact, and GS strategists stay constructive on 2027. His key distinction is that the last forced seller leaving is not the same as the next committed buyer arriving with a fresh risk budget. The question has shifted from 'will AI spending grow?' to whether it can keep delivering earnings acceleration, valuation support and investment returns.
items.angle: A cleaner positioning reset gives you a floor, not a catalyst. With CTAs and HFs de-grossed, the upside driver has to be new money, and in December that's mostly buybacks and pension rebalancing.
items.tweetA: 'The last forced seller leaving isn't the next buyer arriving.' Systematic funds are flat, hedge funds have de-grossed, and the hedges are already monetized. So who's buying at higher prices in December? Buybacks, and that's it.
items.tweetB: Both GS and UBS in the same weekend: positioning reset, technicals fine, lean constructive. When the two biggest equity desks agree the flush is done, the next surprise usually comes from the asset class they don't cover: credit.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Sachs Tony Pasquariello
items.title: Capex, depreciation and future profitability are nearing a turning point, and credit is getting selective on AI infra financing
items.idea: The AI boom delivered an extraordinary earnings windfall, but Pasquariello flags that the relationship between capital spending, depreciation and future profitability is approaching a potentially important turning point. Meanwhile, the credit market is becoming 'considerably more selective' about financing the underlying infrastructure. The balance between positioning, corporate issuance and increasingly ambitious earnings forecasts suggests the next 12 months could reward investors very differently from the last 12.
items.angle: This is the depreciation wave. Capex spent in 2024-26 turns into P&L expense in 2027, just as the financing gets pricier. Issuance supply plus D&A drag together are the bear case for hyperscaler EPS.
items.tweetA: For two years capex was a cash-flow story and earnings looked great. In 2027 it becomes a depreciation story. The GPUs bought in 2025 start hitting the income statement just as credit gets picky. That's when the EPS bar gets tested.
items.tweetB: Goldman and UBS both flag the same thing independently: credit is getting selective on AI infra. Two equity desks pointing at the bond market in one weekend tells you where the real risk is.

charts.desc: Charts inside, worth opening (likely capex vs D&A).

items.title: The 'everything that isn't AI' rotation: a claimed +28% YTD vs Nasdaq-100 +3% and S&P +5%
items.idea: In an end-of-sale promo email, Market Sentiment claims its portfolio is up 28% YTD vs +3% for the Nasdaq 100 and +5% for the S&P 500 (as of Nov 27). It credits early calls on memory, advanced packaging and optics as AI bottlenecks, plus a September pivot ('the next great AI trade is everything that isn't AI'). The next step it signals is buying downstream AI companies, funded by selling something. Treat the performance as self-reported marketing.
items.angle: The useful datapoint is the index level: by its numbers the NDX is up only about 3% YTD in late November, which means the AI liquidation erased almost the entire year. And retail-facing newsletters are now rotating toward 'downstream AI' (adopters, not builders).
items.tweetA: Nasdaq-100 +3% YTD with a month to go, in the year Anthropic went public at $1.2T. The AI build-out kept accelerating and the index holding the builders went almost nowhere. That's what a multiple reset looks like.
items.tweetB: The 2026 winners weren't 'AI'. They were the bottlenecks: memory, packaging, optics. The 2027 pitch from the newsletter crowd is already 'downstream AI', the adopters. When the rotation narrative gets marketed with a 50%-off coupon, it's not early anymore.
